options: "Pretty Good Privacy" — a real-world encryption program mixing symmetric and asymmetric cryptography
A blockchain-specific cryptocurrency
A type of consensus algorithm
A programming language for smart contracts
questions.explain: PGP predates blockchain and is one of the most popular real-world uses of public/private key cryptography, securing emails and files.

questions.q: When encrypting a PGP message, whose public key do you use?
options: The recipient's public key
Your own public key
The recipient's private key
No key is needed to encrypt
questions.explain: You encrypt using the recipient's public key — only their matching private key can decrypt it back to the original message.

questions.q: What do you need to decrypt a PGP-encrypted message?
options: Your own private key
The sender's public key
Nothing — encrypted messages decrypt themselves automatically
The recipient's public key
questions.explain: Decryption requires your own private key, since the message was encrypted specifically using your public key.

questions.q: When signing a PGP message, what do you actually use?
options: Your own private key and your passphrase
The recipient's public key
The recipient's private key
A shared password known to both parties
questions.explain: Signing uses your own private key (unlocked with your passphrase) — the opposite direction from encrypting, which uses someone else's public key.

questions.q: What does it prove if someone successfully verifies your PGP-signed message using your public key?
options: That you specifically signed it, and the text hasn't been altered since
That the message has been encrypted
Nothing meaningful — verification doesn't actually prove anything
That the recipient has read the message
questions.explain: A valid verification confirms both who signed the message and that its content hasn't changed since — the same authenticity and integrity guarantees from Chapter 2.
